summary: Defines Structure of Management Information Version 2 (SMIv2), the adapted subset of the ASN.1 notation used to describe MIB modules, and assigns a set of administrative values. It is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1902.

eli5.summary: This sets the grammar for writing down the lists of things that network devices can report, so every list is written the same way.

what is the difference between counter32 and gauge32
subtitle: The grammar and rulebook for writing down the managed objects that network devices expose through SNMP.

tldr.problem: Network management needs every vendor and working group to describe managed objects in the same machine-readable and human-readable way, with names that never collide or change meaning.
tldr.mechanism: SMIv2 defines an adapted subset of ASN.1 with three macros (MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE, NOTIFICATION-TYPE), a set of base data types, rules for conceptual tables, and a tree of OBJECT IDENTIFIER names rooted at the Internet subtree.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 58) that obsoletes RFC 1902, and it governs how MIB modules are written and revised. The language itself has no security impact.

today: RFC 2578 is an Internet Standard (STD 58) published in April 1999 and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 1902 and is companion to RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

sections.title: What the SMI Defines
sections.content:
Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects living in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). Related objects are grouped into MIB modules, and those modules are written in an adapted subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One, ASN.1 (1988).

The Structure of Management Information (SMI) is the document that defines that adapted subset and assigns a set of administrative values. It has three parts: module definitions (the MODULE-IDENTITY macro), object definitions (the OBJECT-TYPE macro) and notification definitions (the NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro). For exposition, the earlier SMI from RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215 is called SMIv1, and this one is SMIv2.
sections.eli5: It is a rulebook for describing the things a network gadget can tell you about itself, so everybody writes the descriptions the same way.

sections.title: Information Modules and Macros
sections.content:
An information module is an ASN.1 module that defines network management information. The text names three usual kinds: MIB modules (using OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE), compliance statements, and capability statements for agent implementations. The last two use macros from the companion document, RFC 2580. New macros must not be defined inside SMIv2 modules, SMIv1 macros must not be used, and the ASN.1 EXPORTS statement is not allowed because everything defined in a module is automatically exported.

Every module starts with exactly one MODULE-IDENTITY invocation, placed right after any IMPORTS. It must carry LAST-UPDATED, ORGANIZATION, CONTACT-INFO and DESCRIPTION, and it may carry repeated REVISION clauses, most recent first, each with its own DESCRIPTION.

Each macro use looks like descriptor macro clauses ::= value. A descriptor starts with a lower-case letter, uses letters and digits, must be unique and must not exceed 64 characters (over 32 is not recommended). A STATUS clause says whether a definition is current, deprecated (obsolete, but still allowed for interoperability) or obsolete (should not be implemented).

The text stresses that macro expansion happens conceptually during implementation, not at run time.
sections.eli5: Every list of things starts with a title page saying who wrote it and when it changed. After that, each thing gets a name, a description and a label saying whether it is still in use.

sections.title: The Naming Hierarchy
sections.content:
Every managed object is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an ordered list of non-negative numbers called sub-identifiers. In SMIv2 a value has at most 128 sub-identifiers, each at most 2^32-1 (4294967295), and the first one is a well-known name: ccitt (0), iso (1) or joint-iso-ccitt (2).

The Internet subtree is { iso 3 6 1 }, written 1.3.6.1. Under it, mgmt(2) holds standard objects, experimental(3) holds objects being designed by IETF working groups (moved under mgmt when a module becomes a standard one), and private(4) holds objects defined unilaterally, with enterprises(1) beneath it for providers of networking subsystems to register their products.

An OBJECT IDENTIFIER is used for registration or for assignment. After a registration, the meaning of the value can never change, the value cannot be reused, and the descriptor cannot be changed or attached to anything else.
sections.eli5: Names work like a street address that gets more specific with every number, such as country, city, street and house. Once a house number is given to someone, it is never handed to anyone else.

sections.title: Base Types for Object Values
sections.content:
The SYNTAX clause of an object must be a base type, the BITS construct or a textual convention. The base types are three built-in ASN.1 types (INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER) and eight application-defined types: Integer32, IpAddress, Counter32, Gauge32, Unsigned32, TimeTicks, Opaque and Counter64.

A Counter32 only goes up until it reaches 4294967295 and then wraps to zero. A single counter value carries no information on its own, so counters have no defined initial value, cannot have a DEFVAL, and must not appear in an INDEX clause. A Gauge32 can rise and fall between a minimum and a maximum but does not stick at either end. Counter64 may be used in standard modules only if the quantity would wrap in less than one hour with Counter32.

TimeTicks counts hundredths of a second between two epochs. IpAddress is an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte-order, kept for historical reasons. Opaque is for backward compatibility only and no object in a standard MIB may use it.
sections.eli5: Each box on the form has a type: a whole number, a piece of text, a number that only ever goes up like a car odometer, or a number that goes up and down like a thermometer.

sections.title: Conceptual Tables, Rows and Instances
sections.content:
Management operations apply only to scalar objects, but the SMI lets designers imagine a conceptual table. A table has syntax SEQUENCE OF EntryType, a row object has the EntryType syntax, and the columns are the objects beneath the row. Tables and rows are not-accessible. The row's name is the table's name plus sub-identifier 1, and each column's name appends a unique positive sub-identifier to the row's name.

A scalar object's instance is its name with a sub-identifier of zero appended. A column's instance is identified through the INDEX clause of its row. Integer indexes add one sub-identifier, fixed-length strings add one per octet, and variable-length strings add a length sub-identifier first unless the IMPLIED keyword is used on the last index object. An IpAddress index adds 4 sub-identifiers.

As an alternative to INDEX, an AUGMENTS clause says a row has a one-to-one relationship with an existing row and shares its indexing. For rows that allow creation, there should be one column with syntax RowStatus and access read-create, called the status column. The MAX-ACCESS values, from least to greatest, are shown below.
sections.eli5: A table is like a class roll: each row is one student and each column is a fact about them, such as name or age. The index says which row you mean.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
The NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro defines the content of an unsolicited transmission of management information, carried in either a SNMPv2-Trap-PDU or an InformRequest-PDU. Its optional OBJECTS clause lists object types that must each appear, in the stated order, in every instance of the notification. The listed objects must not be not-accessible, and the description must say which instance of each object is meant. An agent may append extra objects at the end.

For compatibility with SNMPv1 traps, the next-to-last sub-identifier in the name of any newly defined notification must be zero. The RFC's own example is entConfigChange, whose description says an agent must not generate more than one such trap-event in a five second period and that a management station should check entLastChangeTime to detect missed ones.
sections.eli5: Most of the time you ask the device questions. A notification is the device tapping you on the shoulder to say something happened.

sections.title: Revising an Information Module
sections.content:
Modules may be revised, but not in any way that could cause interoperability problems between an implementation of the old specification and one of the new. Any change must update the MODULE-IDENTITY (the LAST-UPDATED clause and a new REVISION and DESCRIPTION pair). A module name should not change, definitions should not move to another module, and obsolete definitions must not be removed because their OBJECT IDENTIFIERs must never be re-assigned.

Allowed object changes include adding enumerations or renaming labels, moving current to deprecated or obsolete, adding or updating DEFVAL and REFERENCE, adding UNITS, appending columns to a row, clarifying the DESCRIPTION, and defining entirely new objects. Anything else that changes semantics requires a new OBJECT IDENTIFIER value. Changing a descriptor counts as a semantic change, because descriptors appear in IMPORTS.

Syntax can only be narrowed in limited ways, for example raising a lower bound or lowering an upper bound on an integer range or a string size. Appendix A gives the sub-typing grammar, and ranges in a single clause may touch but not overlap.
sections.eli5: You may fix typos and add new rows to the list, but you may never reuse an old number for a different meaning, because other people's lists point at it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. It says the document defines a language with which to write and read descriptions of management information, and that the language itself has no security impact on the Internet.
sections.eli5: This is only a rulebook for writing things down, so it does not create a security risk by itself.
